title: Arjuna's fear for the family
hook: Arjuna fears a war will wipe out the ways a family keeps: kuladharma
carry: dharma lives in what a family keeps
tomorrow: how does chapter one end: with a battle, or a man sitting down?

segments.voice: Yesterday, still reading the Gita's first chapter, Arjuna said na kankshe vijayam: I don't want victory, Krishna. And kim, what for, was left hanging in the air between the armies. Now he names what he's afraid of losing.

A photo lands in the family group chat: a recipe card in a great-grandmother's handwriting, the corners soft, a turmeric stain on one edge. Within minutes, three cousins want it. Nobody is fighting about the food. They're fighting about what goes missing if the card does. Cut to a chariot between two armies. Arjuna has just told Krishna he doesn't want to win, and he hasn't stopped talking. He's reached a new fear, and it isn't about the men who will die. It's about what dies after them.
screen: `A RECIPE CARD IN THE GROUP CHAT.` → `WHAT GOES MISSING WITH IT?` → `ARJUNA, STILL TALKING.`

segments.voice: Here's his line: kulakshaye pranashyanti kuladharmah sanatanah. Find the seams. Kulakshaye is kula, family, plus kshaya, ruin: in the ruin of a family. Pranashyanti: they perish. Kuladharmah: kula again, plus dharma, so a family's dharma, the duties and rites a family keeps. Sanatanah: long-standing. When a family is ruined, its long-standing ways perish. Here's one to tell someone tonight. Some Hindus today call their whole tradition sanatana dharma. In this verse, sanatana isn't a name. It describes the ways one family keeps. The verses after it carry the fear further: when dharma is lost, disorder overtakes the family, and the rites for the ancestors, the offerings of rice and water, go undone. Now the teaching under the grammar. Dharma isn't only a law written in a book. Hindus keep it at home: the lamp lit at dusk, the shraddha rites for the ancestors, the prayer a grandmother taught. That's kuladharma, and it's why Arjuna's fear is real. Readers hear him two ways. Some hear real grief for everything a war erases beyond the dead. Some hear a frightened man reaching for any argument that might stop the fight. Krishna will answer with another dharma, Arjuna's own duty. But the fear itself names something every Hindu home knows.
screen: `KULA + KSHAYA: IN A FAMILY'S RUIN.` · `KULADHARMAH: A FAMILY'S DHARMA.` · `THE LAMP, THE RITES, THE PRAYER.` · `DHARMA IS KEPT AT HOME.`

segments.voice: On any scrap of paper, write by hand one small way a family you love keeps: a dish, a greeting, a prayer, how a lamp gets lit. Underneath, write whose hands it came through. If you pray, say their names. Then set the pen down and breathe with the page in front of you.
Kuladharmah sanatanah: a family's long-standing ways, the dharma Arjuna fears a war will erase. Reading the Gita's first chapter, one line at a time.

howItsDone: Many Hindu families keep household rites handed down through generations, such as a lamp lit at dusk and shraddha rites for the ancestors: the kind of family dharma Arjuna names in chapter one.

fork.setup: your cousin says dharma is just a big word from old books. what does Gita 1.40 show her?
options: dharma also lives in a family's ways: the lamp, the rites, the prayers kept at home.
dharma only means the law of the universe; it has nothing to do with families.
dharma means whatever a family happens to like doing.
fork.reveal: kuladharmah: a family's dharma. Arjuna's fear is that a war will end the rites and ways a household keeps.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: kuladharma, family dharma, a compound of kula, family, and dharma.

trapdoor: what you thought: sanatana always names the Hindu tradition.
what it means: in 1.40 it describes kuladharmah, a family's long-standing ways, at risk in war.
what a scholar hears: an adjective agreeing with kuladharmah, ancient or perpetual, said of family custom, not a name for a tradition.
recall: victory, which Arjuna says he doesn't want

adharma.meaning: the loss or opposite of dharma; disorder

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 1.40–1.44 (when dharma is lost, adharma overcomes the family; the chain Arjuna fears, including rites for the ancestors)

notes: 1.41–1.43 speak of the corruption of women and the mixing of varnas; the script summarizes them as the chain reaching 'later generations' and does not quote them. A Keeper should judge whether this summary is fair.
'Some Hindus use sanatana dharma as a name for their tradition' is a general statement about modern usage; confirm wording.
The two readings of Arjuna's argument also appear in year one (day 160); here they are kept to two sentences and the day's focus is the compound.

Sanskrit is given in a simple romanization in the spoken text (no diacritics) so the voice can read it; the sources hold the same romanization. Confirm every word against a standard edition, and the verse numbers (editions differ by a verse around 1.27-1.28).
Grammar is described in plain words; a Sanskritist should confirm each description.
